clinicalPearls: Cardiomyopathy denotes primary disease of the heart muscle itself; strictly it excludes myocardial dysfunction secondary to other cardiovascular disease, though common usage also folds in ischemic, valvular, and hypertensive cardiomyopathy.
The traditional morphologic scheme recognizes three major phenotypes: hypertrophic (HCM), dilated (DCM), and restrictive (RCM) cardiomyopathy.

HCM is characterized by increased left ventricular wall thickness (roughly 13-15 mm depending on context) with a normal or high ejection fraction; LV chamber volume is normal or smaller, and EF is usually above 0.60.

DCM is defined when LVEF is at or below 0.50, although most patients present clinically with LVEF at or below 0.40; an LVEF persistently at or below 0.30-0.35 is the threshold considered for primary-prevention ICD.

RCM is the least common phenotype and is defined more by physiology (moderate-to-severe diastolic dysfunction and/or elevated cardiac filling pressures) than by morphology; wall thickness is often increased but may appear normal, EF is usually only mildly reduced, and marked atrial enlargement with predominant right heart failure is typical.

Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC, originally arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia) is a fourth, predominantly genetic phenotype marked by life-threatening arrhythmias and abnormal RV structure/function with variable LV involvement.

Evolving genotype-driven terminology reframes arrhythmogenic disease as ACM-RV (RV-predominant, formerly ARVC), ACM-LV (LV-predominant), and biventricular arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy; in ACM-LV ventricular arrhythmias can dominate before LVEF is severely reduced, so primary-prevention ICD may be considered even with LVEF above 0.35.

Phenotypes overlap and shift over time: DCM can undergo reverse remodeling toward higher EF and smaller ventricles with recommended therapy, and about 5% of HCM evolves to a reduced-EF, more restrictive state (HCM-rEF).
Mid-range LVEF (0.40-0.50) commonly represents a transition state, either deterioration from early DCM or improvement into DCM remission.
Clinical expression frequently follows a two-hit model in which an inherited predisposition is triggered by an acquired insult such as infection, toxic exposure, pregnancy, or tachycardia.

Echocardiography is the initial imaging modality; cardiac MRI adds tissue characterization, with late gadolinium enhancement mapping fibrosis and T1/T2 mapping identifying focal and diffuse inflammation.

Left ventricular noncompaction is a trait (often assessed by a noncompacted-to-compacted myocardium ratio above 2.3) that can accompany HCM, DCM, dystrophies, and syndromes, but can also appear in normal hearts, in pregnancy, and more often in athletes.
harrison.pathophysiology: Cardiomyopathy reflects intrinsic disease of the myocardium producing characteristic structural and functional abnormalities. In HCM, abnormal myocyte/sarcomere biology drives increased wall thickness with preserved or supranormal systolic function but impaired filling. In DCM, the ventricle dilates with depressed systolic function (low LVEF). In RCM, the dominant abnormality is impaired ventricular filling from a stiff myocardium causing markedly elevated filling pressures and atrial enlargement, often with relatively preserved EF. Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy involves fibrofatty or fibrotic remodeling that creates a substrate for ventricular arrhythmias with variable RV and/or LV structural change. An expanding catalog of pathogenic genetic variants underlies heritable cardiomyopathy, and inherited differences in immune-response pathways contribute to infectious and noninfectious inflammation that can manifest as myocarditis and cardiomyopathy. Clinical disease often requires a second acquired insult superimposed on a genetic predisposition.
additionalDifferentials: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) and its variants of LV hypertrophy: asymmetric septal, sigmoid/inverse septal, concentric, and apical hypertrophy
Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), including arrhythmogenic ACM-LV which usually presents with a DCM phenotype
Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy: ACM-RV (ARVC), ACM-LV, and biventricular forms
infectionMimics: Chagas' disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) protozoal myocarditis, which can produce an arrhythmogenic phenotype (ACM-RV/ACM-LV)
Clinical myocarditis from infectious inflammation that can mimic or trigger a cardiomyopathy phenotype
nonInfectiousMimics: Athlete's heart (mimics HCM and can show LV noncompaction)
Aortic stenosis (mimics HCM and should be excluded)
Cardiac amyloidosis (causes RCM and can produce asymmetric septal thickening mimicking HCM, especially in older patients)
Storage diseases mimicking HCM morphology: GLA/Anderson-Fabry, PRKAG2, and LAMP2/Danon disease
Cardiac sarcoidosis (often DCM-pattern or regional wall-motion abnormalities, or RV involvement with arrhythmias, rather than classic restrictive morphology)
Coronary artery disease/prior infarction and primary valve disease as structural causes mimicking DCM
Radiation, scleroderma-type connective tissue disease, and drugs such as doxorubicin causing an RCM phenotype
PVC-related cardiomyopathy versus genetic ACM in patients with frequent PVCs or nonsustained VT
additionalInvestigations: Two-dimensional and Doppler echocardiography as first-line imaging
Cardiac MRI for late gadolinium enhancement (fibrosis) and T1/T2 mapping (focal and diffuse inflammation)
Multigene cardiomyopathy panel with genetic counseling; detailed family history of cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, conduction disease, tachyarrhythmia, and sudden death

Chemistries including sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, glucose/glycohemoglobin, creatinine/BUN, albumin and liver tests, lipid profile, TSH, serum iron and transferrin saturation, creatine kinase isoforms, and cardiac troponin
Hematology including CBC with differential, total eosinophil count if abnormal, and ESR
Targeted infection workup when suspected: HIV, Chagas', Lyme and other tick-borne disease, toxoplasmosis, trichinosis; respiratory pathogen panel in acute respiratory syndromes
Endomyocardial biopsy (with electron microscopy sample) when a specific diagnosis with therapeutic implications is suspected
Coronary angiography/catheterization in patients with evidence of ischemia or infarction who are candidates for intervention
redFlags: Ventricular tachyarrhythmias or nonsustained VT, which may dominate before EF is severely reduced in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy
Family history of sudden death, cardiomyopathy, conduction disorders, or skeletal myopathy
Embolic events from atrial fibrillation or apical ventricular thrombus as a presentation of unrecognized cardiomyopathy
Progressive exertional breathlessness, fatigue, orthopnea, edema, and abdominal symptoms indicating the congestion syndrome
Marked wall thickening suggesting amyloidosis, inherited storage disease, or inborn metabolic disease
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the specific phenotype and underlying cause rather than on classification alone. DCM may improve substantially with reverse remodeling on guideline-directed therapy, whereas about 5% of HCM deteriorates to a reduced-EF, restrictive state. Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy carries a risk of life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias that can precede heart failure. Persistent severe LV systolic dysfunction (LVEF at or below 0.30-0.35) identifies patients considered for primary-prevention ICD.
pitfalls: Treating 'congestive heart failure' as a diagnosis or etiology; it is a nonspecific congestion syndrome common to many cardiac conditions (including congenital heart disease, primary pulmonary hypertension, and valve disease) and requires full etiologic evaluation.
Over-relying on morphologic phenotype, since phenotypes overlap and shift over time and many entities (sarcomeric variants, storage diseases) can present as either HCM or RCM.
Missing amyloidosis in older patients, where it can both cause RCM and mimic the asymmetric septal thickening of HCM.
Misclassifying sarcoidosis as restrictive when it more often produces DCM-pattern, regional wall-motion abnormalities, or RV involvement with arrhythmias.
Failing to distinguish PVC-related cardiomyopathy from a genetic arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy that itself causes both the arrhythmias and the muscle disease.
Interpreting LV noncompaction as inherently pathologic, since it can occur in normal hearts, in pregnancy, and in athletes.
harrison.severityClassification: Morphologic/functional classification: Hypertrophic (HCM) - septal thickness >=15 mm in men, >=13 mm in women (13-14 mm may suffice in relatives of a proband or with a positive genetic test), LVEF normal or high (usually >0.60), normal/small LV volume. Dilated (DCM) - early: LVEF <=0.50 and/or LV end-diastolic volume >112% of normal for age/sex or LVEDD >95th percentile; LVEF <=0.40 is the threshold for traditionally recommended heart-failure therapy; persistent LVEF <=0.30-0.35 is the threshold for primary-prevention ICD. Restrictive (RCM) - functional diagnosis based on moderate-to-severe diastolic dysfunction and/or elevated filling pressures, usually mildly reduced LVEF, with marked atrial enlargement. Mid-range LVEF (0.40-0.50) represents a transition zone. Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy - ACM-LV (usually DCM morphology), ACM-RV/ARVC (2010 modified task force criteria combining major and minor criteria), and biventricular forms. LV noncompaction trait assessed by noncompacted/compacted ratio >2.3.
